The Molecular Speculator In 1827 the botanist Robert Brown was staring down his microscope at a drop of fluid. There were tiny particles in the fluid, and he noticed that they weren't sitting still: they were jumping about in a very erratic fashion. The particles weren't alive, moving under their own volition; and the fluid was absolutely still. What was the cause? Brown suggested that this movement is evidence for the molecular nature of matterwhich at the time was itself a highly speculative theory. The fluid is composed of tiny molecules, whizzing about at high speed and colliding randomly with each other. When the molecules bump into a particle, they give it a random push. It is possible to model Brownian motion by a 'continuous' random walk. This is defined by taking a discrete version, with small time-steps and small individual movements in many directions, and then passing to the limit. William Feller describes what this achieves: In the limit the process will occur as a continuous motion. The point of interest is that in passing to the limit our formulas remain meaningful and agree with physically significant formulas of diffusion theory which can be derived under much more general conditions by more streamlined methods. This explains why the random-walk model, despite its crudeness, describes diffusion processes reasonably well.   page_194 Page 195 What we have is a direct mathematical connection between the motions of individual molecules, and the bulk properties of the fluid they make up. The statistical features of molecular motion, and the continuum mechanics of diffusion, agree. The first person to discover the connection between random walks and diffusion was Louis Bachelier, in a doctoral dissertation of 1900.

For all practical purposes, such a fluctuation in a macroscopic system is “impossible.” Probability theory shows that we can expect fluctuations about the equilibrium number density to be on the order of 1N, where N is the number of molecules per unit volume. These fluctuations correspond to continual fluctuations of the entropy about its equilibrium value. Such fluctuations are generally unobservable for systems of macroscopic size but can be detected in special situations (see below). If a system had 100 molecules, we would get fluctuations of about 10 molecules, which is an easily detectable 10% fluctuation. A system of 106 molecules would show fluctuations of 0.1%, which is still significant. For 1012 molecules (⬇1012 mole), fluctuations are 1 part per million, which is perhaps the borderline of detectability. The validity of the second law is limited to systems where N is large enough to make fluctuations essentially undetectable. In certain situations, fluctuations about equilibrium are experimentally observable. For example, tiny (but still macroscopic) dust particles or colloidal particles suspended in a fluid and observed through a microscope show a ceaseless random motion (Fig. 3.14), called Brownian motion (after its discoverer, the botanist Robert Brown). These motions are due to collisions with the molecules of the fluid. If the fluid pressure on all parts of the colloidal particle were always the same, the particle would remain at rest. (More accurately, it would sink to the bottom of the container because of gravity.) However, tiny fluctuations in fluid pressures on the colloidal particle cause the random motion.

#### 1. Introduction

Finding the density for the first time a Brownian motion reaches a moving boundary is an old and classic problem with a wide range of applications in both mathematics and applied sciences. The problem may be traced back to Louis Bachelier's doctoral thesis [Bachelier (1900)], Théorie de la Spéculation, and to a paper by the Austrian physicist Erwin Schrödinger [Schrödinger (1915)].

On the other hand, Robbins and Siegmund (1973) and later Groene-boom (1987), Salminen (1988) and Martin-Löf (1998) are among the first to explicitly establish the relationship between hitting time problems and parabolic partial differential equations.

The aim of this work is not to provide a new set of solutions to the problem of boundary crossing. Our goal is instead conceptual: we establish relationships between (a) hitting time problems of Brownian motion, (b) 3-dimensional Bessel bridge, (c) Schrödinger's equation with linear potential, and (d) heat equation problems with moving boundary. We determine conditions under which these problems are equivalent.

The paper is organized as follows: The hitting time problem is introduced in Section 2, and by use of Girsanov's theorem, we relate it

to a functional of a 3-dimensional Bessel bridge. This relationship is established in Section 3.

Next, in Section 5 we derive a pair of equivalent problems which in Section 6 are used to link boundary crossing probabilities with the heat equation. We conclude in Section 7 with some final remarks.

August 24, 2026

###### Abstract

We investigate first-hitting location (FHL) statistics induced by drift–diffusion processes in domains with absorbing boundaries, and examine how such boundary laws give rise to intrinsic information observables. Rather than introducing explicit encoding or decoding mechanisms, information is viewed as emerging directly from the geometry and dynamics of stochastic transport through first-passage events. Treating the FHL as the primary observable, we characterize how geometry and drift jointly shape the induced boundary measure. In diffusion-dominated regimes, the exit law exhibits scale-free, heavy-tailed spatial fluctuations along the boundary, whereas a nonzero drift component introduces an intrinsic length scale that suppresses these tails and reorganizes the exit statistics. Within a generator-based formulation, the FHL arises naturally as a boundary measure induced by an elliptic operator, allowing explicit boundary kernels to be derived analytically in canonical geometries. Planar absorbing boundaries in different ambient dimensions are examined as benchmark cases, illustrating how directed transport regularizes diffusion-driven fluctuations and induces qualitative transitions in boundary statistics. Overall, the present work provides a unified structural framework for first-hitting location laws and highlights FHL statistics as natural probes of geometry, drift, and irreversibility in stochastic transport.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12147200/)Abstract

While it is very common to model diffusion as a random walk by assuming memorylessness of the trajectory and diffusive step lengths, these assumptions can lead to significant errors. This paper describes the extent to which the physical trajectory of a Brownian particle can be described by a random walk. Analysis of “timelapses” of physical trajectories (calculated over collisional time scales using a velocity autocorrelation function that captures the hydrodynamic and acoustic effects induced by the solvent) yielded two observations: (i) these subsampled trajectories become genuinely memoryless only when their time step is ∼200 times larger than the relaxation time, and (ii) the distributions of the subsampled step lengths have variances that are significantly smaller than the diffusional ones (usually by a factor of ∼2). This last observation is due to two facts: diffusional displacements are mathematically “superballistic” at short time scales, and subsampled trajectories are “moving averages” of the underlying physical trajectory. The counterintuitive result is that the mean squared displacement (MSD) of the physical trajectory asymptotically approaches 2Dt (where D is diffusivity) at long time intervals _t_, but the MSD of the individual subsampled steps does not, even when their duration is several hundred times larger than the relaxation time. I discuss how to best account for this effect in computational approaches.

Abstract

a time-dependent boundary as a function of the boundary. We prove that the
boundary-to-distribution map is infinitely many times differentiable along the

keenable.title: Energy-constrained Brownian motion
keenable.snippet:
For reflected Brownian motion in an interval of length N, we consider the first time at which the length of time since the most recent visit to the boundary reaches M; this random ‘lifetime’ comes from the interpretation in which the Brownian motion has a finite energy capacity M, uses energy at unit rate in the interior, and gets its energy replenished up to M on every visit to the boundary. We prove distributional asymptotics for the lifetime in three different regimes depending on the relative growth of N and M; these one-dimensional results parallel results in the random walk case by Wade and Grinfeld. We also present some initial results on the multidimensional version of the problem, for one scaling regime in the case of a ball, and conjectures on the behaviour in general domains.

In this paper we give a complete picture for the one-dimensional case; in the meagre capacity regime there is a limit theorem with the so-called Darling–Mandelbrot law, in the confined-space regime, an explicit normalization gives an exponential limit, and in the critical regime, the limiting law is characterized by its moment generating function. These one-dimensional results (presented in Section 2) parallel the random-walk results from [20], but also include a non-asymptotic result for Brownian motion on the half-line, where a Darling–Mandelbrot statement holds for fixed parameter values.

The interpretation as an *energy-constrained Brownian motion* comes from associating to the diffusing particle a non-negative energy level. Energy decreases at constant rate when the process is in the interior of the domain, and is replenished to maximal level M whenever the process visits the boundary. The first time at which M units of time have elapsed since the last visit to the boundary is thus the first time at which the energy level drops to zero while the process is in the interior, at which point the process terminates, as it no longer has energy to move.

keenable.title: Moment-optimal Gamma approximation of Bessel Process exit times
keenable.snippet: We construct finite Gamma convolutions approximating the first hitting time of 1 by a Bessel process of index ν>−1 started at the origin. The scale measure in the classical exponential representation of this law is obtained by squaring the positive half of a dilated modified Lommel polynomial orthogonality measure. Its Jacobi recurrence yields an N-factor Gamma convolution that uniquely matches the first 2N cumulants, the maximal number attainable in this class. From an exact Gaussian quadrature remainder we derive supergeometric convergence of the Laplace transforms on compact subsets of a common slit plane and geometric convergence of the distribution functions uniformly on the real line. The approximants have total Gamma shape N(N+ν+1), and their Laplace transforms and negative moments decrease to those of the exit law.

keenable.title: Volterra clocks and their pure-jump limits: hitting times of curved boundaries
keenable.snippet:
We introduce a class of continuous Volterra processes, called Volterra clocks, and study their singular limit as the memory kernel collapses to a Dirac mass at zero. The dynamics are parametrised by a function f acting as a nonlinear time-change, generalising the Volterra square-root process and recovering it when f is affine. In the singular limit, the continuous Volterra clock converges weakly to a pure-jump process given by first passage times of a Brownian motion to curved boundaries, including affine and square-root boundaries when f is, respectively, affine or quadratic.

In summary, our results reveal a strong structural connection between stochastic Volterra processes and boundary crossing problems for Brownian motion with curved boundaries. Specifically, our new class of Volterra clocks are shown to be natural continuous approximations of Brownian first hitting time processes in a way that covers a broad range of singular scaling regimes, characterised by the degeneration of memory kernel K(t)dt⇒δ_0(dt). In particular, this allows us to treat several regimes that have been studied separately within a unified framework, including (i) large-time limits (Section 4.1), (ii) fast mean-reversion limits (Section 4.2), and (iii) hyper-rough regimes for fractional kernels with α↓0 (Section 4.3).

| | X_t=(B(e^t))/(e^(t/2)),dX_t=dB_t^′−(1)/(2)X_tdt, | |

## 6. Hitting a Barrier When the Drift Moves  
Section 2 showed that, at a single date, only the integral of the drift matters. Path-dependent quantities are different. Ask when X first reaches a fixed level *b*. Subtracting the drift turns this into a question about plain Brownian motion: σWt must reach the **moving boundary** b − X0 − M(*t*). With a constant drift, M is a straight line, and the [reflection principle](https://riskhub.org/blogs/reflection-principle-for-brownian-motion) plus a change of measure gives the classical Bachelier-Lévy closed form (see [hitting times and their distributions](https://riskhub.org/blogs/hitting-times-and-their-distributions)). For a curved M there is, in general, no closed form. Special shapes such as square-root boundaries have known results, but most desks handle this numerically.  
A practical example is the probability that the fitted Ho-Lee short rate from Section 5 goes negative within 10 years. The rate is rt = f(0, t) + σ2t2/2 + σWt, a Brownian motion against a curved floor.

Title: Generalized Images for Brownian First Passage to Monomial Boundaries

Authors: Gerardo Hernández-del-Valle

View PDF HTML (experimental)

Abstract: We study the first passage of Brownian motion to a monomial moving boundary. For every integer degree at least two, we construct a time-independent signed image measure whose heat potential is the killed Brownian transition density on a nonzero interval of the natural Brownian time scale. The image density is determined by a second-kind Volterra equation in the image coordinate, not by the classical Volterra equations in time for the hitting density. Its kernel is an explicit Wright function, and the first-passage density is recovered afterwards from the boundary flux. Exponential bounds establish convergence, while a beta-moment transform connects the Wright kernel with the finite-order differential hierarchy previously obtained from transported moving zeros. A cubic numerical experiment independently checks the resulting density against simulated Brownian paths.

seltz.snippet:
Hitting times of Brownian motion beyond one level: two-sided exit probability a/(a+b), expected exit time ab, the Laplace transform as a price, drift and sloped boundaries, and a verified stop-loss and take-profit example.

## Hitting Times and Their Distributions

A hitting time is the first moment a random path touches a set. Most introductions stop at a single level: when does Brownian motion first reach *a*? That question has a clean answer, covered in detail in First-Passage Times of Brownian Motion. This article goes one step further, into the hitting-time questions a trading desk actually asks: which of two levels is hit first, how long the wait is, what a payment made at the hitting time is worth today, and what happens when the boundary itself moves.

## 1. One Level Is Rarely the Question

Picture a trader who buys a stock at 100 with a stop-loss at 90 and a take-profit at 115. The position ends the first time the price leaves the band (90, 115). Three numbers matter to her: the probability that the exit is at 115 rather than 90, the expected time she will be tied up in the trade, and the value today of any payment triggered by the exit. None of these is a single-level question. A credit analyst modelling a firm that defaults when assets fall to a barrier, or a structurer pricing a double-no-touch, asks the same three things.

The plain-English picture is a drunk walker in a corridor with a door at each end. He is certain to leave eventually, because a corridor of finite width cannot hold a random walker forever. The questions are which door he leaves by and how long it takes. The surprising part is how little machinery the answers need: two martingales and one theorem, the optional stopping theorem, which is explained with its conditions in Stopping Times and Their Role in Quantitative Finance. seltz.title: Brownian Motion with Time-Dependent Drift
seltz.snippet:
Brownian motion with time-dependent drift: why X_T stays normal with mean equal to the integrated drift, a full derivation of the Ho-Lee theta(t) = df/dt + sigma^2 t, a worked example repricing zero-coupon bonds, and why path-dependent hitting probabilities depend on the drift's shape.

## Brownian Motion with Time-Dependent Drift

Most introductions to Brownian motion give it a constant drift: a steady push of μ per year, plus noise. Real models rarely stay that simple. The most important place a *time-dependent* drift turns up is in interest-rate modelling, where a drift function θ(*t*) is chosen, date by date, so that a model reproduces today's yield curve exactly. This article explains what changes when the drift becomes a function of time, derives the Ho-Lee drift from scratch, computes it on a stated curve, checks that the model reprices zero-coupon bonds, and then shows the one place where the shape of the drift, and not just its total, matters: barrier hitting.

## 1. Why a Drift That Changes With Time?

Think of a river current. A constant drift is a canal: the water moves at the same speed everywhere, so a floating leaf drifts at a steady rate while wind (the noise) jostles it. A time-dependent drift is a tidal estuary: the current is strong at one hour, weak at another, and may even reverse. The leaf still gets jostled by the same wind, but where it ends up on average depends on the whole timetable of the current.

Finance needs the estuary for three recurring reasons:

- **Fitting a term structure.** A short-rate model with constant parameters produces its own yield curve, which will not match the market's. Letting the drift vary with time gives the model one free number per maturity, enough to hit every point on today's curve.
- **Known future events.** Scheduled central-bank meetings, dividend dates and seasonal commodity patterns all shift the expected path at known times.

### Denis S. Grebenkov

### Laboratoire de Physique de la Mati`ere Condens´ ee,

### CNRS - Ecole Polytechnique, F-91128 Palaiseau, France Email: denis.grebenkov@polytechnique.edu August 20, 2018

#### Abstract The surrounding world surprises us by the beauty and variety of complex shapes

**that emerge from nanometric to macroscopic scales. Natural or manufactured materials (sandstones, sedimentary rocks and cement), colloidal solutions (proteins and DNA), biological cells, tissues and organs (lungs, kidneys and placenta), they all present irregularly shaped "scenes" for a fundamental transport "performance", that is, diffusion. A stochastic differential equation, written the usual way, lives on the whole real line. Interest rates, inventories, queue lengths and pegged currencies do not. For reflected Brownian motion in an interval of length N, we consider the first time at which the length of time since the most recent visit to the boundary reaches M; this random ‘lifetime’ comes from the interpretation in which the Brownian motion has a finite energy capacity M, uses energy at unit rate in the interior, and gets its energy replenished up to M on every visit to the boundary. We prove distributional asymptotics for the lifetime in three different regimes depending on the relative growth of N and M; these one-dimensional results parallel results in the random walk case by Wade and Grinfeld. We also present some initial results on the multidimensional version of the problem, for one scaling regime in the case of a ball, and conjectures on the behaviour in general domains.

In this paper we give a complete picture for the one-dimensional case; in the meagre capacity regime there is a limit theorem with the so-called Darling–Mandelbrot law, in the confined-space regime, an explicit normalization gives an exponential limit, and in the critical regime, the limiting law is characterized by its moment generating function. These one-dimensional results (presented in Section 2) parallel the random-walk results from [20], but also include a non-asymptotic result for Brownian motion on the half-line, where a Darling–Mandelbrot statement holds for fixed parameter values.

The interpretation as an *energy-constrained Brownian motion* comes from associating to the diffusing particle a non-negative energy level. Energy decreases at constant rate when the process is in the interior of the domain, and is replenished to maximal level M whenever the process visits the boundary. The first time at which M units of time have elapsed since the last visit to the boundary is thus the first time at which the energy level drops to zero while the process is in the interior, at which point the process terminates, as it no longer has energy to move.
